newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria says SS-23 missiles essential to defence.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria says SS-23 missiles essential to defence.

text.p: Bulgaria said on Thursday it was reluctant to destroy its SS-23 Spider missiles as proposed by the United States because they formed an important part of its defences.

A Defence Ministry spokesman said Defence Minister Georgi Ananiev and Armed Forces Chief of Staff General Miho Mihov had stated that destroying the missiles "did not correspond to the interests of Bulgaria".
"This would lead to a serious imbalance between the armaments of Bulgaria and its neighbours," he said.
Under the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty, Bulgaria declared eight SS-23s, plus 36 mobile launchers for Scud missiles, the predecessor of the SS-23, and 28 launchers for Luna missiles.

The SS-23 missiles, with a range of 500 km (310 miles) and accurate to within 30 metres (yards), have the ability to deliver nuclear warheads but Bulgaria says it has never had nuclear weapons on its soil.
The Russian-made missiles were also supplied to former East Germany and Czechoslovakia but have been withdrawn.

"The United States is very concerned at the proliferation of ballistic missiles," said Paul Beaver of Jane's Defence Weekly. "Intermediate range missiles pose a potential threat especially as there is no defence against them."
He said Bulgaria's neighbours, Romania, Greece, Turkey and Hungary, no longer had ballistic missiles.
Military sources in Sofia said that, if Bulgaria scrapped the missiles, its main defence alternative would be an air strike capacity which its tactical battlefield airforce lacks.
The Balkan state of 8.4 million people has applied to join NATO but lacks the funds to modernise its armed forces.
The U.S. embassy in Sofia confirmed that the question of scrapping the missiles had been raised with the Bulgarian government but said it was not putting any pressure on them.

"The same issue has been raised in the past few years with other foreign governments and with previous Bulgarian governments as part of our global effort to reduce the world supply of missiles capable of handling weapons of mass destruction," a statement said.
"This was in no sense an ultimatum, a demand or an effort to exert pressure but an inquiry to ascertain Bulgaria's current thinking, conveyed at a low level," it said.
